title: Rebuilding the Student Safety Net
summary:
Rebuilding the Student Safety Net
Joshua.Bay Thu, 10/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new report examines emergency aid programs in seven states, highlighting how eligibility rules, application processes and other design choices shape students’ access to assistance.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
A rent increase, car repair or unexpected medical bill can create financial disruptions that threaten a student’s ability to stay enrolled in college. Research has shown that emergency aid—often provided through modest grants of $500 to $1,000—is a promising way to prevent such financial setbacks from derailing a student’s progress toward a degree.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal support delivered through the Higher Education Emergency Relief Fund demonstrated how emergency aid could serve as a safety net when funded at scale. But since that funding expired, the availability of emergency aid has contracted sharply.

The share of students who reported receiving emergency aid fell from 44 percent in fall 2021 to just 4 percent in fall 2025. That nearly 90 percent decline comes at a time when basic needs insecurity remains widespread and changes to public benefits and financial aid under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act threaten to place additional financial strain on students.

As such assistance has dwindled, a new report from the Hope Center for Student Basic Needs at Temple University examines how seven states are taking different approaches to helping students navigate financial emergencies.

Mark Huelsman, director of policy and advocacy at the center and author of the report, said states are playing an increasingly important role in filling gaps in emergency aid as federal support recedes, especially as demand for assistance remains high.

“States being the home of emergency aid is a relatively new phenomenon. They’re trying to fill the gaps for students … at a time when federal support broadly is very tenuous,” Huelsman said. “But the need for emergency aid spikes when institutions and students have the fewest resources to address the needs.”

How states differ: The report examines statewide emergency aid programs in California, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and Washington, finding considerable variation in eligibility requirements, allowable expenses, application processes and reporting practices.

For Huelsman, the findings highlight how the design and administration of emergency aid programs can influence whether students receive assistance when they need it most.

“We saw a real value in simplicity and trust with students,” Huelsman said. “So minimizing the barriers to entry and having proactive outreach to say to students, ‘Look, things happen, unexpected expenses come up, this is a common occurrence, you’re not alone, and we’re going to make it as easy as possible to get aid quickly.’”

He added that emergency aid programs should account not only for unexpected bills, but also for sudden losses of income or other financial resources that can leave students struggling to cover basic expenses.

“Being as broad and flexible with the uses of emergency aid, or the reason students could access emergency aid, is really promising and important,” Huelsman said. “We’re seeing states and colleges continuing to build out ecosystems of basic needs supports on their campus, and having emergency aid truly embedded in that is something that we’re hopeful will continue.”

A lasting safety net: Huelsman said one challenge for states and institutions is to balance limited emergency aid funding with the need to make students aware that assistance is available.

“Institutions or states working with extremely limited resources don’t want to overpromise and underdeliver,” Huelsman said. “But withholding some outreach is, by definition, going to make it so that many students who could use it may not access the program.

“Our recommendation at the end of the day is to make students aware of these programs because it helps with the advocacy for growing the programs,” he added. “If all of the emergency aid is gobbled up in the first semester because students are experiencing a ton of emergencies, that tells you that the program probably needs more funding.”

As more states consider establishing emergency aid programs, Huelsman said such assistance should be part of broader efforts to address college affordability and students’ basic needs.

“There’s no bad place to start with emergency aid,” Huelsman said. “It should be part of a more comprehensive solution on affordability. It should sit alongside expanding financial aid. It should sit alongside expanding student access to existing public benefits and other resources.”

“Too often it’s thought of as an afterthought or stopgap,” he added. “But there’s infrastructure from which states and institutions can start.”

title: Longtime Legal Advocate Decries ‘Coordinated Assault’ on Noncitizens’ Rights
summary:
Longtime Legal Advocate Decries ‘Coordinated Assault’ on Noncitizens’ Rights
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 10/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

Thomas A. Saenz, president and general counsel of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, first began advocating for in-state tuition for undocumented students in 1993.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
When Thomas A. Saenz first began working on the issue of tuition equity in 1993 at the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, “whether undocumented students could pay [in-state] tuition or not was more or less an open question.”

But over the course of the next decade, after federal law was decided and, with the help of groups like MALDEF, states began passing laws that permitted undocumented students to qualify for in-state tuition based on certain factors, the situation for these students became more clear.

Saenz, now the president and general counsel of MALDEF, said, “From a legal perspective, this was settled.” In 2024, 24 states and Washington, D.C., allowed undocumented students who met certain criteria, such as having gone to high school in the state, to pay the in-state rate.

But, after the Trump administration’s Justice Department filed 25 lawsuits in the last 16 months, in-state tuition for undocumented students has been rolled back in at least six states and remains uncertain in many others.

The DOJ argues that these state policies violate a 1996 law that bars noncitizens from qualifying for higher education benefits, such as in-state tuition, on the basis of residence unless “a citizen or national of the United States is eligible for such a benefit.” Offering in-state tuition to undocumented students incentivizes illegal immigration and disadvantages U.S. citizen students, the administration claims.

Saenz and many other immigrants’ advocates disagree. They argue that the policies are legally sound because they allow undocumented students to qualify for in-state tuition based on many factors, sometimes not even including residency, and they often include factors that permit U.S. citizen students from other states to also qualify for in-state tuition.

Advocates say it’s only fair to allow undocumented students—the vast majority of whom were brought to the United States as young children—to pay the same tuition rates as the citizen students they grew up alongside at the colleges they mutually earned admission to. These students often go on to graduate, gain work authorization and make great contributions to their communities, they say.

And it’s not a violation of federal law. Of that, Saenz, who has been working on the issue since before the federal law or any of the state policies came into existence, is sure.

Saenz spoke with Inside Higher Ed about his experience working on the nation’s first tuition-equity policies, what in-state tuition means for undocumented students and how the administration’s campaign could end. This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Q: Since these policies first began, what has in-state tuition meant for undocumented students and communities more broadly?

A: It’s made higher education affordable for a lot of people who otherwise would have had to go to a private college and hopefully receive private financial aid, or who would have otherwise not really been able to pursue higher education.

What it has meant for the community is that these graduates—who are graduates because they were able to afford their education—most of them are highly contributing to the economy and society. That’s because many of the students who were undocumented when they came into college now have work authorization either because they’ve adjusted [their status] or because they have authorization through something like deferred action. In either case, they’ve been able to make a very significant contribution to the economy but also to public safety—many of these graduates are in health care or in other front-line occupations.

Q: How did in-state tuition for undocumented students become an issue for state and federal policymakers?

A: In California there were court decisions going in both directions, one that said undocumented students couldn’t receive regular tuition and the other saying they could. Those cases were keyed up by anti-immigrant folks, basically. So that’s what I think partially raised the issue. And then Proposition 187, which included a higher education provision. [Editor’s Note: In 1994, California voters approved Proposition 187, which prohibited undocumented immigrants from benefiting from many public services. A federal judge ruled the measure unconstitutional in 1998.]

I think that’s what put it on the radar of the folks who spearheaded the enactment of the federal restrictions first in the Welfare Reform Act and then subsequently in what is known as Section 1623.

Prior to that, it was very informal. Some schools would allow undocumented students to pay in-state tuition, others might not. But then the federal government stepped in in 1996.

Q: When you started working on this issue and the first policy was being developed in Texas, was there concern about violating the 1996 federal law?

A: From my personal experience, yes. They were absolutely aware. Not only do I know it from my involvement, but I also would note that there is a presumption under federal law and under state law that legislators know the current law when they act. So you actually have to make an assumption when you analyze these kinds of things that the legislators were aware of 1623, and they certainly were.

Both California and Texas took steps to avoid having their policies struck down by 1623. In California, residence is not a criterion at all to receive regular tuition. In Texas, residence is one criteria of several. In neither case is it the only criterion, which is what 1623 would strike down.

No other administration since 2001, when Texas and California enacted their laws, no Department of Justice under an administration of either party, including the first Trump administration, has ever filed a lawsuit challenging these laws. I think that’s also an indicator that everyone understood that because they didn’t rely solely on residence, all of these state laws were compliant with Section 1623.

Q: So, why are they doing it now?

A: Well, I can’t tell you that. Obviously this Trump administration, even in comparison with the first Trump administration, is much more virulently anti-immigrant, and they pursue anti-immigrant policies in every way that they can. This is a particular pernicious step because all of these students are future contributors to the economy and society of their states. They’re much-needed educated members of the workforce.

Q: At a recent press briefing, you mentioned that these lawsuits are just as much part of the administration’s anti-immigration agenda as the Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids and arrests. What do you mean by that?

A: Well, certainly the street enforcement has garnered lots of headlines, as it should because of the extreme brutality, the racial profiling, the deaths. This campaign in court doesn’t get as much headline-grabbing attention because they’re keeping it under wraps.

They are, I believe, seeking to avoid any kind of backlash to this litigation campaign by not publicizing it as a campaign. If you were going to go out and sue nearly half the states in the country, that’s generally something that you would be touting much more and talking about more. They’re not doing that.

Q: Not all of the states are defending the laws, but we’ve seen MALDEF and other groups try to get involved in the suits on behalf of students by filing motions to intervene. I know not all of these petitions have been successful, but can you explain why you took that approach?

A: The federal rules of civil procedure provide for intervention of parties who have an interest that could be impaired by litigation if they are not adequately represented by the others in the case. So you can intervene as a plaintiff or you can intervene as a defendant. In these cases, we have sought to intervene as a defendant, because in many of these cases the states are not putting up any defense.

This would be the quintessential situation where the intervention should be allowed. The state is not defending a law in which our clients have a very strong interest because it’s what makes higher education affordable for them. Ordinarily these would be easy motions, but we have not been allowed to intervene except in Kentucky. In Texas, the court denied intervention on the basis of futility. In Oklahoma, the district court never ruled. And in Kansas, the court approved the consent decree and therefore denied our motion to intervene, in essence asserting that it was unnecessary to grant intervention because the court was at the same time approving the consent decree.

So, other than in Kentucky, there has been a failure to apply the correct law to allow students, who are those most directly affected by the attempted elimination of tuition equity, to intervene—which is what should be allowed.

Q: You’ve mentioned that MALDEF and others could petition the Supreme Court to review the decision in the Texas case. What would that look like?

A: Technically, because the Fifth Circuit panel has continued to deny our intervention, our clients aren’t parties to the case. If we had been granted intervention, our clients would be parties to the case. But they’re not, and when you’re not a party, you don’t really have the ability in federal court to challenge a decision.

What they decided and what would go to the Supreme Court is whether intervention should have been granted. Now, if intervention is granted, then we could come back and ask to challenge the merits of the consent decree. But right now that’s not something we can technically do.

There is a way in which they overlap, because the Fifth Circuit decision was based on futility. That means the Fifth Circuit decided our arguments on the merits were not good at all, and therefore it would be futile to allow us to intervene. There’s a way the current status does lead to some potential analysis of the merits issue, but technically the first issue—and the only issue at this time—is whether intervention should have been granted.

Q: You’ve referred to the 25 lawsuits as a coordinated assault on the rights of undocumented students. Did this coordinated assault surprise you?

A: Well, they followed Texas pretty quickly with Oklahoma, so they indicated pretty early on that they would be filing more lawsuits. But was I surprised in the first instance? Absolutely. As I said, no administration has ever filed a lawsuit challenging these laws. Clearly, they have a different view of the law than their predecessors. That was surprising.

Initially, we might have thought they would leave out the California model [in which residence is not a criterion], but they filed in California fairly quickly as well. That’s because they have this really unsupported theory that attending high school in the state is the same as residence, when it plainly is not in practice. But that’s their claim.

In my mind, that clearly identified it as a coordinated assault.

Q: We saw advocates condemn the lawsuits, but we didn’t see as much forceful language about the administration’s campaign. Was there a specific reason why you waited? Do you think the legal advocacy community was prepared for this fight?

A: Honestly, I think we expected the media to write about this as a coordinated assault, but when it became clear that the media, by and large, is generally treating these as one-offs, we concluded that we need to be more forceful in pointing out the pattern that clearly indicates a coordinated assault on these students and these laws.

Prior to Texas, I don’t think this was top of mind as a prospect of the overall anti-immigrant policies of this administration. There were so many other things going on, and I don’t necessarily think that anybody anticipated this. Again, it is so unique in the history of these laws.

Q: Besides dealing with these lawsuits, what’s next on advocates’ lists in the fight for college access for undocumented students?

A: I think that there are still political battles even if we prevail. For example, in Oklahoma, we were already on appeal when the Oklahoma Legislature and governor repealed the law. There’s nothing we can do about that. So, our lawsuit in the 10th Circuit in Oklahoma is only for that period of time when students were paying higher out-of-state tuition because of the consent decree. But once the [repeal] legislation took effect, there is nothing we can do.

So there is still an ongoing need to reinforce political support.

title: Universities Are on an AI Philosopher Hiring Spree
summary:
Universities Are on an AI Philosopher Hiring Spree
kathryn.palmer… Thu, 10/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

Artificial intelligence is raising existential questions about knowledge and humanity—and creating exploding demand for philosophy professors equipped to investigate them.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
The job market for humanities scholars may be bleaker than ever—except for the handful of academics who specialize in the philosophy of artificial intelligence.

Although a small subset of philosophers have long worked at the intersection of science and technology, the rapid integration of generative AI into daily life over the past four years has heightened demand for their expertise. Philosophy departments across the country have already hired faculty for new, AI-specific positions, and a quick scan of the online job board PhilJobs.com shows that the trend isn’t slowing down. So far this fall, more than a dozen philosophy departments—including at Purdue University, the University of Illinois at Chicago and the Georgia Institute of Technology—have announced searches for AI-focused tenure-track faculty.

“While other humanities disciplines have much to offer in our current technological transition, too, philosophy is uniquely well suited to address the full range of needs and challenges posed by the rapid development and adoption of AI technology today,” said Cameron Buckner, who became an endowed chair in the philosophy of AI at the University of Florida in 2024. That’s because the existential questions AI is raising—such as what it means to have a mind and what constitutes knowledge—“are questions that philosophy classes have always explored,” he said. “Philosophers can contribute a great deal of value to these conversations.”

‘Hunger’ to Understand

College students looking for answers to those and other questions about how AI may influence their futures are part of what’s fueling the AI-philosopher hiring spree.

“There is a great hunger amongst the undergraduates to understand how the world is shifting under their feet, perhaps more rapidly than at any other time in history than perhaps the Industrial Revolution,” said Buckner, adding that his department has no trouble filling seats in its undergraduate ethics, data and technology course. “They recognize that they are subjects in a worldwide experiment in turning over vast swathes of human thinking to machines whose inner workings we barely understand.”

The creators of these powerful AI systems are also interested in what philosophers think. In recent years, numerous philosophers have left academe to work in research labs at companies such as Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta. For instance, since 2021, New York University–trained philosopher Amanda Askell has been working for Anthropic, shaping what she calls “the soul” of its large language model, Claude.

“At this point, half of my friends in the [field] have already been scooped up by one or another big tech company to go do something very similar to what they were doing in the academy, but now at the forefront of AI research,” Buckner said. Although companies with philosophers on staff have occasionally eschewed research showing potential downsides to their products, in most cases “not only do they listen to the philosophers, they offer them wheelbarrows full of money and place them in leadership positions to drive their research agenda.”

For philosophy departments, the urgency to understand AI also presents an unusual opportunity to hire more faculty—so long as their research engages AI.

“It’s wild. I've never seen one area so dominate what [philosophy departments] are looking for,” said Joshua Thurow, chair of the philosophy and classics department at the University of Texas at San Antonio. “A lot of people are having a hard time getting hires approved by their administration. Departments are just looking for something that the administration is going to be excited about, and AI is the thing that every university is excited about right now.”

That excitement enabled Thurow to make his department’s first tenure-track hire in years just before the start of this fall semester; UTSA received money from the state to hire a cross-discipline cluster of faculty members to study AI and education, including one philosophy position.

A ‘Foolish Waste’?

However, philosophy departments may not be producing enough qualified applicants to meet the ballooning demand for AI philosophers.

As in most humanities fields, both the pool of philosophers and available faculty jobs have shrunk over the past 10-plus years. According to data from the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, between 2011 and 2022 the number of completed doctoral philosophy degrees across the United States fell from 580 to 477. And only a fraction of those graduates have expertise in AI-related subfields.

“Philosophy of technology has been a less emphasized area among most of the top 50 Ph.D. programs in the United States,” Thurow said. “Consequently, I think a lot of programs were sort of ill prepared to meet this demand. Now they’re changing fast.”

But not every philosopher welcomes the field’s embrace of AI.

Brian Leiter, a philosophy professor at the University of Chicago School of Law, called the trend “a foolish waste of philosophy lines, no doubt partly a result of administrators hopping on the bandwagon and pressuring departments to find warm bodies” in a blog post last week. “Why not give the lines to specialists in the post-Kantian Continental traditions, which are a magnet for students … and in whom interest is strong across disciplines?”

At the same time, faculty who have been hired as a result of surging interest in AI say this moment is a chance for the field to spotlight the practical applications of studying philosophy.

“AI raises some really profound questions about the nature of the mind, knowledge, language, aesthetics and other areas that turn out to be quite salient in both the design and use of the technology,” said Heidi Furey, the associate professor of philosophy at UTSA who was hired to research AI, ethics and education as part of the cross-campus cluster. “Philosophy used to be the thing that was nice to think about if you had the time, interest and inclination. People are starting to see it as fundamental to the whole thing.”

title: You Can’t Build Golden Science Without Global Talent
summary:
You Can’t Build Golden Science Without Global Talent
sara.custer@in… Thu, 10/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

Trump has announced millions in funding for new science and tech initiatives, but the anti-immigrant America First agenda could undermine his ambitions.

Byline(s)
Sara Custer
full_text:
At a gilded ceremony at the Institute of Peace last week, President Trump announced a $6 billion investment in a new “golden age” of American science. The project promises resources for “high-potential” American STEM students and early-career researchers, investments in scientific instruments and computing power, and a nuclear-powered spacecraft set to take off for Mars in 2028.

After nearly two years of shifts and cuts to federal research funding, new investments in science and tech fields offer reasons to be optimistic. But the same administration is throttling the flow of foreign talent needed to maintain the country’s leading position in the global tech race.

Consider a recent report from the Hoover Institution and the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. Researchers argue that in a world of increasing tech competition, talent is “a strategic vulnerability that is easy to miss.” Strategic fields such as AI and biotechnology “rely critically on one input that cannot be stockpiled, export-controlled, or manufactured on demand,” the report says. “That input is people.” The battle fought in classrooms, laboratories and immigration queues “will have as much to do with who leads the technologies of the next half-century as any arsenal.”

The report’s authors analyzed the current supply of STEM talent in the U.S., from high school graduates to postdocs. The study notes that even before American students leave high school, their math proficiency lags behind their peers in other countries. Across all global assessments, American K–12 math scores have plummeted over the past 20 years and now sit below global averages. Not only is the country’s STEM foundation weak, but researchers also identified a “wide but leaky” talent pipeline filled with domestic STEM students at the bachelor’s level that turns increasingly foreign the higher you climb on the credential ladder.

According to the National Science Foundation, nearly 300,000 temporary visa holders were enrolled in science and engineering master’s and Ph.D. programs in 2025. For decades, the U.S. has successfully retained foreign graduate students, many of whom go on to contribute to American innovation through entrepreneurship and careers in STEM industries. SanDisk, Instagram, OpenAI and Grammarly are among the billion-dollar companies whose founders included former international students.

But international educators worry that the administration’s clampdown on international students will make keeping their talent in the country more difficult. Last week, the Department of Homeland Security released a plan to charge institutions $70,000 for each foreign student participating in the work program optional practical training. The two-year extension for STEM students will cost an additional $30,000. DHS said the fee is a matter of national security and an effort to root out fraud in OPT. The agency expects to see a smaller pool of participants as a result of the policy.

In the global race to dominate tech innovation, losing American-educated foreign STEM talent is also a national security threat of its own. Nearly 100,000 STEM graduates were authorized to work through OPT last year. If a portion of them attend institutions that can’t or won’t pay tens of thousands of dollars for them to participate in the program, their lost workforce contributions won’t be readily filled by domestic STEM graduates.

The Hoover/HAI report also found that domestic STEM students often don’t launch careers in STEM industries, while foreign STEM graduates, who are required to work in industries related to their field of study, do. “You cannot replace an international Ph.D. with a domestic Ph.D. one-for-one, because domestic Ph.D.s are substantially less likely to work in STEM,” researchers wrote. Their numbers show a 19-percentage-point gap in STEM education-to-employment conversion rates between domestic and foreign graduates. “Every international Ph.D. who leaves takes a fraction of a position with them that no domestic replacement fills.”

Not only do domestic graduates enter STEM careers at a lower rate, Americans who start STEM degrees don’t tend to finish them. The millions of dollars Trump says he will invest in American science education and STEM Ph.D.s is unlikely to result in a surge of American scientists. From 2003 to 2011, only about one in four American students who started a STEM degree actually graduated with one, according to the report. That share held steady despite massive investments in science over that period. “Across nearly a decade in which STEM enrollment grew, federal science funding rose and public policy debates recognized the importance of technical education, the share of entrants converted into STEM graduates did not budge,” the report notes. “Whatever filters students out has been operating at the same rate for years, unchanged by the growth in funding or enrollment.”

Our greatest global competitor, China, is also dumping billions of dollars into science as a strategic priority. China already dominates research in crucial fields such as nuclear energy and outperforms the U.S. in key research metrics—notably citations and spending. China’s labs are stocked with American-educated scientists who were pulled back home by lucrative jobs or pushed out of this country under Trump’s anti-China policies. And while the U.S. is closing its doors to foreign talent, China is sending a different message: After the Trump administration announced a $100,000 fee for H-1B visas (a federal judge vacated the plan in June, but the administration announced another $100,000 fee in August), China rolled out its K-Visa for foreign STEM graduates from “well-known” universities. During his visit last month, Chinese President Xi Jinping stood at the White House and invited 100,000 American students to China for educational exchanges.

Boosting American innovation through investments in government, universities and industry partnerships makes strategic sense. And the resources are sorely needed after the government slashed research funding and continues to upset the normal order of awarding grants. But it’s not enough. The government will find it near impossible to regain America’s leading role in global innovation without the world’s best minds working in our universities and labs. The anti-immigrant priorities of the America First agenda stand to tarnish the golden age of science before it even begins.

title: Why small colleges are closing and the toll on students and communities
summary: Across the nation, scores of small private colleges and universities are either closing or under threat. As each school shutters, students, faculty, and the surrounding community struggle to find a way forward. Paul Solman reports on one such school and the effects of its demise. It's part of our higher education series, Rethinking College, and produced in collaboration with the Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Amna Nawaz:

Across the nation, scores of small private colleges and universities are either closing or under threat. With each shuttering, students, faculty, and the surrounding community struggle to find a way forward.

Tonight, Paul Solman reports on one such school.

This story was reported in collaboration with The Hechinger Report and is part of our higher education series Rethinking College.

Tommy Lee Jones, Actor:

The answer you're looking for lies right here.

Paul Solman:

Box office sensations.

Lupita Nyong'o, Actress:

I would make a great queen because I am so stubborn.

Paul Solman:

Award-winning actors.

Narrator:

We have shared the incommunicable experience of war.

Paul Solman:

PBS' most celebrated documentarian.

The common thread, all grads of a little liberal arts school in Massachusetts, Hampshire College, founded in 1965 as an experiment, no grades, no required classes, students designing their own curriculum.

Ken Burns, Documentary Filmmaker:

I don't recognize the person who entered Hampshire College in the fall of 1971 and the person who graduated in the spring of 1975.

Paul Solman:

Filmmaker Ken Burns.

Ken Burns:

It just rearranged all my molecules. I don't think I would be talking to you as a documentary filmmaker and so many other things if Hampshire hadn't provided the kind of preparation that it had.

Jim Wald, Former Hampshire College Professor:

We would teach people to be thinkers about profound issues of knowledge and society, and that way they would be adaptive learners who could carry on this process of individual thinking as they pursued careers and so forth.

Paul Solman:

History professor Jim Wald taught at Hampshire for nearly 40 years.

Jim Wald:

When it opened, it was the hot place, I'm told, more selective than Harvard or equally selective as Harvard. Hampshire was always way up there in really making students do a lot of work, because the idea was to show people how to be scholars. This is what it means to be a historian or a biologist.

Paul Solman:

Or become a filmmaker like Barry Sonnenfeld or writer like Jon Krakauer.

Jim Wald:

Our students were challenged much more than others in a lot of other schools. The college has a Latin motto, non satis scire, to know is not enough, embodying this idea of wisdom and critical thinking.

Paul Solman:

An ethos that persisted for actors like Lupita Nyong'o of the "Black Panther" and "The Odyssey" and Liev Schreiber.

Liev Schreiber, Actor:

Hampshire was interested in radical questions. The faculty and the other kids were interested in things that were different. Challenging the world in which you live in, in a positive and constructive way was certainly the ethos.

Paul Solman:

And students like Chloe De Lisle today, finishing her thesis in ethnomusicology.

Chloe De Lisle, Hampshire College Student:

I'm looking at the process of when sound in film becomes part of the music and how that represents a protagonist's trauma.

Paul Solman:

What would be an example?

Chloe De Lisle:

"Apocalypse Now" and how the signature helicopter sound that really permeates the film is part of the protagonist's experience and trauma, and then a collective cultural trauma.

Paul Solman:

Ken Burns' final thesis 51 years ago?

Ken Burns:

My half-an-hour film called "Working in Rural New England" for Old Sturbridge Village, which is a living history museum.

Paul Solman:

So you mean you literally began your career doing what you have been doing ever since at Hampshire?

Ken Burns:

It's even worse than that, Paul, which is the last shot of the film for Old Sturbridge Village was a pan across a painting from an agrarian to a kind of industrial or preindustrial sequence.

Paul Solman:

Just like so many pans in his PBS films, and thus Hampshire's hallmark from then to now, focused exploration.

Chloe De Lisle:

Here has allowed me to really do whatever I want and really create my own major, and that's meant everything. And I have just gotten to pull all my interests together and create something really cool.

Paul Solman:

A result of deep connection with the school.

Mars Richman, Former Hampshire College Student:

With the class structure, without those prerequisites, able to do what you want, chart your own course, I feel that I was able to be focused faster than most people would at a traditional college.

Paul Solman:

First year student Jupiter Brady-McCullough feels the same.

Jupiter Brady-McCullough, Former Hampshire College Student:

I made some great friends. I had some really amazing classes with some really amazing professors, and I learned a lot about myself. So I think I'm not alone in feeling kind of hopeless, in that we see a lot of these small schools closing right now.

Paul Solman:

And this barren scene on Hampshire's campus could become a reality for scores of schools across the country. One analysis finds that, in the next decade, of the nation's 1700 nonprofit private colleges and universities, more than 400 are on the brink, meaning the nearly 700,000 students projected to go to them are at risk.

In fact, when Hampshire announced last April that it would be closing at the end of this year...

Mars Richman:

I cried all day. Everyone cried all day. We were...

Paul Solman:

Really? Everybody?

Mars Richman:

Everybody cried all day long.

Paul Solman:

But you knew that school had been in trouble?

Mars Richman:

We all -- I mean, we all knew, but it kept not dying. Logically, we all knew someday it would, but it kept kind of escaping death.

Madeline Keating, Hampshire College Student:

Hampshire means everything to me.

Paul Solman:

Madeline Keating is finishing up her study in fiber arts.

Madeline Keating:

I was pretty devastated like everybody else, but I also had an understanding that this was kind of coming.

Paul Solman:

That's because the writing had been on the wall for years. Hampshire almost went under in 2019, a young school, a meager endowment, reliant on student tuition in the era of the great college squeeze, says Hampshire President Jennifer Chrisler.

Jennifer Chrisler, President, Hampshire College:

Hampshire, like many institutions of a higher education today, faced a real firestorm between enrollment, cost of college, the changing demographics across this country, the pressure on the value of a liberal arts degree.

Paul Solman:

Fewer high school seniors, fewer going to college, dizzying costs, and a scary job market. No wonder Hampshire teetered. Finally, last April:

Jennifer Chrisler:

When it became clear that we couldn't deliver the kind of education that we knew was the most consequential for our students, we decided to do the responsible thing and teach out in a way that allowed those students who wanted to graduate with us to be able to do so, and those who needed to pursue transferring to another college or university the time to be able to do so.

Paul Solman:

Down from a height of more than 1,200, 170 mostly seniors are sticking it out until graduation. But on the 820-acre campus, that's almost five acres per student. What's happened to those who've left? Some have transferred.

Mars Richman:

I didn't plan on going to college after high school.

Paul Solman:

But Mars Richman did.

Mars Richman:

I heard about Hampshire, and I thought that it sounded like the school of my dreams. I felt really lucky to be somewhere it felt like I was actually getting the support I needed to be able to learn.

Paul Solman:

He finished two years at Hampshire in April. After the school announced it would close, he'd become confident enough to transfer to the nearby University of Massachusetts at Amherst, student body 30,000.

You wouldn't have gone to UMass Amherst out of high school, right?

Mars Richman:

Absolutely not, no.

Paul Solman:

But did Hampshire prepare you for this?

Mars Richman:

As far as being in a higher education institution, yes, absolutely.

Paul Solman:

But when colleges like Hampshire close, many students leave higher ed altogether.

Peter Stokes, Huron Consulting Group:

Research suggests that, when a student is at a college that closes, only about 50 percent of those students actually reenroll at another college.

Paul Solman:

Peter Stokes is a higher education researcher.

Peter Stokes:

And, of those, only about 50 percent complete. So a college closure is exceptionally disruptive to the lives of students.

Paul Solman:

Is Hampshire then the cliched canary in the coal mine?

Jupiter Brady-McCullough:

I applied to three schools, Sterling College, Hampshire College, and College of the Atlantic, and two of them are now closed.

Paul Solman:

As just this year are both Hampshire and Sterling, a fate now threatening to befall hundreds of colleges across higher ed, 500 of which have closed in just the last 10 years.

For the "PBS News Hour," Paul Solman in Amherst, Massachusetts.

title: A Democratic Reckoning in India
summary: The battle on the streets over the foundations of the state.
full_text:
India is in rebellion. At stake is the very future of the country’s democracy and the potential of its renewal. The mass protests that have unfolded in Delhi since July and flared again this month are nothing less than a contest over the foundations of the Indian state and whether it lives up to its constitutional commitments.

Demonstrations began in the summer as students decried perceived unfairness in the country’s examination system. They have now widened to a struggle over the integrity of India’s elections, after authorities began to purge over 130 million people from draft voting lists over the last year. Many of those stripped from the electoral rolls are appealing their removal—an often laborious process—but the possibility of mass disenfranchisement is real. Tens of thousands of mostly young people have taken to the streets in Delhi in the past week, with protests now spreading to other major cities. The demonstrators are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner and questioning the credibility of India’s ostensibly independent institutions. And they are holding Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi directly responsible, accusing him of “stealing democracy.” In their rejection of the country’s current trajectory, the protests pose the most significant challenge to Modi’s authority since the prime minister came to power in 2014.

The main opposition parties, which have never come close to dislodging Modi in national parliamentary elections, put up a united front under Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the Congress party, and an impressive show of force at a rally in Delhi on October 12. But the real heart of the protest is the intense political energy and inventiveness shown by Gen Z students. These young people have defied prohibitions on protest, breached draconian security clampdowns, and endured detentions to relentlessly question the government’s authority.

The government, for its part, also sees this confrontation as an existential battle. This is evident in its determination to contain the protests, deploying over 40,000 security personnel, closing down metro and train stations, barricading central Delhi, suspending mobile Internet, and detaining over 7,000 people. It has doggedly defended the chief of the Election Commission and it has refused to talk to the opposition or the youthful protesters about their demands.

Modi is in no danger of falling; this will not be a rerun of recent Gen Z protests in neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal that successfully toppled governments. But the Indian government faces a subtler danger: its writ no longer carries unequivocal sway. A strongman such as Modi likes to project unquestioned personal authority. Since 2014, his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has consolidated and centralized power to an unprecedented degree. For the government, the open defiance of young people—who come from all class, religious, and caste backgrounds and cannot easily be dismissed or stigmatized as belonging to an “antinational” group—is an unprecedented challenge. It makes the Modi government’s once adamantine grip on power seem more fragile. The future of Indian democracy hinges on whether this contest opens up more democratic space or leads to greater repression.

THE PROMISE OF EQUALITY

Modern India is founded on two legitimizing institutions: elections and exams. Since its independence in 1947, India has maintained a reputation for conducting free and fair elections. The Election Commission of India, an independent constitutional body, has sweeping powers to ensure that the polls remain beyond reproach. The credibility of the commission has been central to the credibility of Indian democracy.

India also conducts recruitment for public-sector jobs and admissions to public and several private colleges through competitive national exams. For millions of young people, the stakes in these exams are high. Success can send candidates scrambling up the ladder of opportunity, but failure can consign them to never climbing it at all. It is important, therefore, that these exams be conducted fairly and have the imprimatur of honesty and impartiality.

India remains a doggedly unequal society in which money, kinship, and power distort almost all institutions. In this context, elections and exams are the only two processes that make the state’s promise of equal treatment tangible. Elections give even the poorest Indians the prospect of dignity and agency, and as a result, voter turnout rates are routinely high. Exams sustain a parallel promise: they keep alive the idea that academic diligence and performance can trump other forms of social capital. To be sure, the staging of both elections and exams has never been perfect, but the overall integrity of the processes has never been in doubt.

Over the last year, however, the actions of the Indian government have cast doubt on elections and exams. In 2024, the main nationwide entrance examination for medical schools was engulfed in controversy over a slew of irregularities, including the advance leak of the exam’s questions. Protests ensued, and students raised serious questions about the reliability of the examination system. The episode also put the National Testing Agency, the central body that under Modi had become responsible for conducting many important exams, under intense scrutiny. Centralization was meant to ensure greater efficiency and regularity. Instead, it made the crisis deeper by concentrating responsibility at the level of the federal government. In July, antigovernment protests forced the resignation of the education minister over frustrations with the examination system.

Similarly, over the last year or so, the Election Commission decided to undertake what is known as a Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, an assessment of India’s voter lists to ensure their accuracy. The exercise is well within the powers of the Election Commission; the last such revision was conducted between 2002 and 2004. But the process has become quite controversial this time because of concerns that it places excessive burdens on citizens to prove their eligibility to vote; the lack of transparency about why names are being added or deleted from the lists; and the use of new software that has given the Election Commission the ability to strip citizens from the voter rolls on trivial grounds, often overriding established procedures and the recommendations of those local officials who do the actual verification.

According to his critics, Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner, acted unilaterally and recklessly in pursuing the revision of voter rolls in ways that violated normal procedures. Since June 2025, the SIR has tagged roughly 130 million names for removal from the voter rolls. Although many of the deletions were duplicates and the names of people who had died or left the country, millions of Indians have found themselves stripped of the right to vote and now burdened with the difficult task of appealing to a tribunal to prove their citizenship. In this light, the protests have already had one constructive effect: the election commission is trying to placate its critics by making it easier for those excluded to lodge appeals.

Gandhi has alleged that the SIR is an instrument for manipulating elections. Already, in the state of West Bengal, where nine million names were taken off, millions of Indians found themselves unable to participate in state elections in March because their appeals were yet to be heard. The elections brought Modi’s BJP to power in the state for the first time. But even if the Election Commission is not systematically targeting voters based on their identity or their political preferences, the exercise still risks disenfranchising millions through sheer ineptitude.

To make matters worse, India’s Supreme Court, another vital democratic institution, has also played an unfortunate role in this train of events. The Supreme Court effectively collaborated in the disenfranchisement of voters in West Bengal by blithely claiming that those whose petitions were under appeal could just vote in the next election after their appeals had been adjudicated; it didn’t matter if they missed voting in the current election.

The sense of the Supreme Court’s callousness was compounded in May after Surya Kant, the chief justice, compared a group of young lawyers pressing for change to “cockroaches.” That stray remark precipitated a social movement, with the creation—initially as a joke but then in earnest—of the “Cockroach Janata Party,” a group that has galvanized young Indians both on social media and in the streets. It played a key role in forcing the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, in July, after mass protests in Delhi and across the country. It is now driving young Indians to call for the resignation of Kumar, the chief election commissioner.

Most significantly, it has linked the credibility crisis directly to Modi, encouraging a veritable explosion of public mockery of the prime minister on social media and the Internet. That has punctured Modi’s carefully cultivated image of an invincible leader who delivers on every promise. He has prided himself on his dominance of social media, but the loss of control over the political narrative, especially on the image-sharing platform Instagram, was palpable. The prime minister has feebly tried to make his own reels in response, but that failed to stem the tide of public irreverence. The ridicule was noteworthy not simply as political satire. It lifted the pall of fear that had hung over Indian democracy since Modi became prime minister, as critics have been silenced through intimidation and opposition leaders targeted through legal proceedings. In mocking power, young people found their voice.

The threat they pose to Modi is significant. These young Indians are not saddled with the historical baggage of ties to conventional opposition parties. The issues they focus on—exams and elections—cut across social divides and even partisan political affiliations. And the protesters’ grit, wit, inventiveness, and fearlessness have dented Modi’s authority like nothing else has in the past 12 years.

THEIR OWN FUTURE

The movement must still contend with the brute reality of state power, which has been evident in the streets of Delhi this past week. Authorities tried to physically suppress and contain dissent by prohibiting it and preventing protesters from entering certain public spaces. That in turn has given young Indians another reason to go to the streets, to protest the right to protest and reclaim public spaces. The government has deployed thousands of security forces in the national capital, as if it were facing some invading foreign army, not young people making reasonable demands, and all signs are that Modi will continue to maintain a hard line on the protests.

For the government, the movement’s principal demand, the resignation of Kumar, is not simply a question of one official’s tenure. Modi has secured extraordinary loyalty within his BJP through an implicit assurance that those who act at the government’s behest will be protected from the consequences of their actions. If that assurance begins to fray, ministers and party functionaries may worry about what might happen when they can no longer take for granted the protection of the leadership. Modi’s defense of Kumar, then, may be less about the SIR than about preserving loyalty to the government within the ranks of his party.

Moreover, Modi has built much of his political persona around turning perceived slights into demonstrations of strength. To yield in the face of public mockery would be especially difficult and out of character. Kumar’s removal could be read as an admission of guilt. Such a retreat could then embolden Modi’s rivals and encourage further protests—and raise the prospect that a galvanized opposition might finally unseat the prime minister in the next parliamentary elections scheduled for 2029.

The danger facing the Indian government is that it comes to believe its own propaganda.

To be sure, the future electoral consequences of the protests remain uncertain. Public anger does not automatically translate into votes. The Election Commission may yet blunt the controversy by admitting voters whose appeals are pending or by making procedural concessions that reduce the immediate grievances. The BJP may still benefit from a fractious opposition and from the fact that voters in a country as large as India are rarely united in their motivations and perceptions of the political stakes. The next major electoral test, in the state of Uttar Pradesh, is still some months away, in March 2027. A victory there for the BJP would allow the party to claim that its authority remains intact; a defeat would make it much harder to contain the political implications of the present controversy. The government is likely to double down on repression against dissenters nationwide, trusting that it can succeed in limiting public expressions of anger.

The BJP is hoping that the more disruptions there are in Delhi, the more it can cast the current upheaval as the work of rabble-rousers and anarchists and rally Indians behind the prime minister. The government and its supporters are already seeking to discredit the movement as the work of foreign hands, invoking conspiracy theories and examples of alleged malign foreign intervention in the youth demonstrations in Bangladesh and Nepal that ousted sitting governments.

Yet the greater danger facing the Indian government is that it comes to believe its own propaganda and ignores genuine discontent. In both Bangladesh and Nepal, the depth of popular grievance was obvious for anyone willing to look—as it is in India. Despite India’s headline growth rates, young people worry about their economic future. Graduate unemployment is at 23 percent, white-collar job growth has slowed to a creeping one percent this year, and nearly a quarter of Indians between the ages of 15 and 29 are not in employment, education, or training programs. The very institutions that were meant to secure their future—elections, courts, and independent agencies—are losing their trust. The strongman is failing, even as the opposition struggles to inspire a great deal of conviction and enthusiasm. What is powerful about this moment, then, is the spectacle of young people who, lacking many good options, are still choosing to fight for their democracy the only way citizens can when it is in peril: with energy, aspiration, and the belief that they can craft their own collective future, wherever that may lead.

title: Ireland’s international education sector risks hitting “social license wall”
summary:
Housing pressures, perceptions of racism and concerns over graduate outcomes risk undermining public support for international students, panellists at the second edition of The PIE Live Ireland have warned.

The post Ireland’s international education sector risks hitting “social license wall” appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Ireland’s international education sector risks hitting a “social license wall” if universities continue to expand without sufficient public support, experts have warned, pointing to concerns over housing, student experience and graduate outcomes.

At The PIE Live Ireland earlier this week, Jess Lister, director of education at Public First, said Ireland ranked highly in an EU-wide poll on whether a university degree was an impressive achievement, but respondents were less supportive of increasing international student numbers.

“The university system merrily cracks on with what it’s doing – educating students, growing, building degrees, bringing more people in – and you eventually [hit] a kind of social license wall,” she said.

Housing pressures, concerns about educational quality and graduate outcomes, and questions around community and belonging could all contribute to that resistance, Lister added.

Chris Rawlings, senior partner at Voyage, presented an analysis of online conversations and search behaviour suggesting that perceptions of international students in Ireland were comparatively negative across the markets his organisation tracks.

The university system merrily cracks on with what it’s doing – educating students, growing, building degrees, bringing more people in – and you eventually [hit] a kind of social license wall

Jess Lister, Public First

He said international student concerns about racism and exclusion were prominent, particularly in conversations involving Indian students, alongside issues such as employment, accommodation, course quality and return on investment.

Rawlings stressed that the data was not a substitute for representative polling, but argued that it offered a real-time indication of how prospective students and local communities were discussing international education.

“One of the things we’re seeing is that, unlike elsewhere, the conversation between local and international students is often negative,” he said, adding that some Indian students were warning others against coming to Ireland.

Celestine Rowland, managing director of Galway Business School and Galway Cultural Institute, said international education is increasingly becoming part of wider migration debates, despite students’ contribution to local economies and communities.

International students were among the most visible groups affected by population growth, but had little voice in public debate.

Rowland also warned that an over-reliance on particular recruitment markets could make students more visible and vulnerable to criticism.

Diversifying international student populations, she suggested, could help reduce the tendency to associate particular groups with local pressures.

She added that housing remains a significant concern – but stressed that international students should not be blamed for a shortage driven by wider population growth and other pressures.

The discussion also highlighted the tension between universities’ reliance on international student fees and their responsibility to maintain public trust.

Jonny Johnston, policy and research adviser at Trinity Global, said institutions needed to demonstrate the value international students bring to research, innovation, teaching and campus life.

But he argued that sustainable public funding was also essential to reducing universities’ dependence on international fees. It follows the news that Ireland’s higher education sector faces a funding shortfall of more than €250 million.

A funding model that leaves institutions reliant on recruitment income risks undermining the student experience, suggested Johnston, particularly if universities lack the resources to support teaching and student services.

Lister similarly questioned whether institutions could maintain public trust if financial pressures left them prioritising recruitment over student outcomes.

“If your incentive is, ‘I have to do this thing, otherwise I can’t run my institution’, you just chase the recruitment,” she said.

Rawlings warned that dependence on a small number of source markets could also leave institutions vulnerable as international student preferences and destination markets change.

He pointed to shifts in markets such as China, where growing domestic education capacity and alternative destinations could affect demand, arguing that focusing too heavily on one market was unlikely to be a sustainable long-term strategy.

Lister also urged institutions to demonstrate the contribution international students make to the wider economy, including through work in healthcare and teaching, entrepreneurship and participation in local projects.

“It’s just joining the dots in a lot more systematic way, rather than keeping it as ‘we do international recruitment over here, and we have our little paradigms over here,’” she said.

Johnston said universities needed to communicate their contribution to research and innovation more consistently, while recognising that messaging alone would not resolve the structural challenges facing the sector.

Rowland pointed to initiatives at Galway Business School and Galway Cultural Institute that bring students into contact with local businesses through industry weeks, projects addressing business needs and volunteering. She said these activities were beginning to support students’ links with employers and their prospects after graduation.

However, Lister cautioned against relying on promotional messaging without addressing the issues communities are experiencing.

In a climate of economic pressure, she said, institutions risk a backlash if they simply highlight their achievements without explaining how their work benefits the wider public.

title: Community-Guided Teaching: Building Relationships Before Course Design
summary:
A Relational Framework for Community-Guided Teaching in Higher Education  In higher education, many instructors want to include Indigenous perspectives, experiential learning, and community-engaged approaches in their courses, but they are not always sure how to begin. Yet the question is not only whether this work should be done, but how it should be done. Without […]

The post Community-Guided Teaching: Building Relationships Before Course Design appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
A Relational Framework for Community-Guided Teaching in Higher Education

In higher education, many instructors want to include Indigenous perspectives, experiential learning, and community-engaged approaches in their courses, but they are not always sure how to begin. Yet the question is not only whether this work should be done, but how it should be done. Without ongoing consultation with Indigenous community partners, Indigenous content can be added symbolically rather than relationally. University timelines can also pressure educators to move quickly toward course outcomes before trust and community guidance have had time to develop.

This article grew out of a collaboration between Safieh Moghaddam, a non-Indigenous professor at the University of Toronto Scarborough; Carol Ducharme, an Indigenous colleague and Assistant Director of the Indigenous Initiatives Office; and Elders from Curve Lake First Nation, whose guidance shaped the work. Through this process, the authors learned that meaningful engagement develops slowly through listening, trust, community guidance and a willingness to let relationships shape the direction of teaching.

A critical consideration before beginning this work was Safieh’s recognition, as a non-Indigenous educator, that good intentions were not enough. She understood the importance of approaching the work with humility and positioning herself as a learner rather than an expert. This required a shift away from the usual role of professor. Instead of leading, planning, and deciding from the outset, she had to slow down and allow the work to be shaped by community relationships. This required courage: the courage to step back and accept that meaningful community-guided teaching begins with learning from others.

This article introduces the Relationship Before Research (RBR) Framework, a reflective approach that emerged through our collaboration with Curve Lake First Nation and later shaped our teaching practices. Rather than beginning with a finalized syllabus, planned experiential learning activity, or course plan, the framework emphasizes community direction, relational accountability, and reciprocity. We do not present the RBR Framework as a universal blueprint or rigid formula. Instead, it offers educators a practical starting point for approaching Indigenous-informed and community-engaged teaching with greater care, patience, and ethical responsibility. Four interconnected phases became central to the teaching adaptation of the framework: listening and relational foundation-building, community guidance and ethical practice, pedagogical integration, and reciprocity and sustainability.

Figure 1 – The Relationship Before Research (RBR) Framework as Applied to Teaching.

Although presented as separate phases, they often overlap and evolve throughout the teaching process.

Phase 1: Listening and Building a Relational Foundation

Safieh’s first instinct was to approach the project the way many academics are trained to: start with a course plan, define learning outcomes, and organize activities for the semester. However, after consultation with Carol Ducharme and collaboration with Elders from Curve Lake First Nation, it became clear that a different approach was needed. This required slowing down, listening carefully, and allowing relationships to guide the process.

In this first phase, conversations with Elders focused on community priorities, respectful engagement, ethical responsibilities, and what meaningful collaboration might look like in a teaching context. Rather than immediately organizing guest lectures or experiential learning activities, the early stages centred on trust and reciprocity. This reflected Wilson’s (2008) concept of relational accountability, where teaching is shaped by responsibilities to the relationships that make it possible.

This phase also reinforced the importance of students learning directly from Elders and community members as well as through guided experiences. Rather than positioning the instructor as the primary authority on Indigenous knowledge, the work emphasized humility, relational learning, and shared guidance.

As trust developed, Elder and community input began to shape decisions about classroom integration, student preparation, reflective activities, journaling, and appropriate ways to introduce Indigenous-informed learning into undergraduate courses. This highlighted the importance of consultation before implementation and relationships before course design.

Phase 2: Community Guidance, Teaching Integration, and Ethical Practice

Consultation could not happen only once at the beginning of the collaboration. As the partnership with Curve Lake First Nation continued to grow, ongoing conversations with Elders and community members remained central to decisions about teaching activities, experiential learning opportunities, and classroom engagement.

Elder and community guidance helped shape the integration of Indigenous-informed learning into undergraduate linguistics courses, including guest lectures, land-based learning opportunities, reflective activities, journaling, and classroom discussions. These were not treated as isolated course additions. Instead, this phase emphasized reciprocity, adaptability, and relational learning. The instructor’s role was not to interpret or represent Indigenous knowledge, but to listen, reflect, and learn under the guidance of Elders and the community.

Questions of ethical responsibility also became increasingly important, including student preparation, classroom reflection, and how community knowledge should be discussed and represented in teaching spaces. The work was informed by OCAP® principles, particularly around consent, accountability, and respectful engagement.

This phase also highlighted the need for responsiveness in community-guided teaching. Rather than relying only on standard university structures or predetermined classroom plans, teaching activities continued to evolve through community input.

Phase 3: Pedagogical Integration

In the classroom, the work invited students to approach language as more than course content. In Safieh’s undergraduate sociolinguistics courses, Elder-led teachings, reflective journaling, classroom discussions, and land-based learning helped students consider language in relation to social life, land, history, oral tradition, identity, relationships, and community knowledge. This approach aligns with Jo-Ann Archibald’s (2008) Indigenous Storywork principles, including respect, responsibility, reciprocity, reverence, holism, and interconnectedness.

One of the most meaningful components was a full-day land-based visit to Curve Lake First Nation, where students spent the day with Elders. They received teachings from Elders who carry this knowledge through lived experience, rather than learning only through abstract concepts or textbook material. The visit invited students to think about language, culture, and knowledge in more relational and land-based ways. Rather than positioning students as passive observers, it emphasized active engagement, responsibility, and community guidance.

This phase also reinforced the importance of careful preparation before community-engaged learning. Before the visit, students participated in discussions and reflective activities focused on positionality, respectful engagement, community protocols, and the historical impacts of colonial education. This helped them enter the space with greater humility, respect, and awareness.

Following the visit, reflection remained central throughout the process. Through journaling, written responses, and discussions connected to Elder teachings and the land-based learning experience, students were encouraged to think critically about language, relationships, community, and accountability. These activities helped them connect course concepts to lived experience in more meaningful ways.

Student reflections suggested that the visit felt different from learning abstract concepts in a classroom. Several students noted that they were not only learning about language, culture, and history, but receiving these teachings from Elders who had lived these experiences and generously shared their knowledge.

For some students, the visit was also deeply moving and healing. It created a stronger sense of connection, respect, and responsibility and helped them understand that learning in this context is not only intellectual, but also relational and ethical.

What This Looked Like in Practice

In practice, this approach included Elder-led guest lectures, classroom discussions, journaling, and a land-based visit to Curve Lake First Nation. Students prepared beforehand through discussions of respectful engagement, positionality, colonial histories, and local protocols. After the visit, they participated in guided discussions and written reflections about language, relationships, accountability, and experiential learning.

Phase 4: Reciprocity and Sustainability

One of the most important lessons from this work is that community-engaged teaching cannot end when a course or semester finishes. Within the RBR Framework, reciprocity means considering how teaching practices and experiential learning can support long-term community priorities. In the Curve Lake collaboration, this meant continuing conversations about how the teaching could evolve in respectful and sustainable ways. Rather than treating Indigenous-informed teaching as a one-time activity or isolated guest lecture, the emphasis remained on accountability, consultation, and long-term collaboration.

Sustainability also involved encouraging students to engage with community-created educational materials, journaling, and discussions that connected classroom learning to broader histories and responsibilities. Ultimately, sustainability is not simply about repeating an activity in a future course. It is about continuing dialogue and remaining accountable to the people and communities who make this teaching possible.

Reflections and Practical Challenges

Implementing community-guided teaching in higher education can be deeply meaningful, but it requires patience, flexibility, and reflection. One challenge is balancing institutional timelines with relational ones. Universities operate through semesters, course schedules, assignment deadlines, and curriculum planning, while relationships develop gradually through trust and continued presence. Educators may therefore need to slow down and avoid moving activities forward before guidance is fully established.

Another important consideration involves reconsidering the instructor’s role. In community-guided teaching, the instructor is not the primary knowledge holder or decision-maker. This requires careful listening, openness to guidance, and recognition of community expertise. For many educators, this means moving away from instructor-centred approaches and creating opportunities for students to learn from Elders and community members.

Accountability must also be part of teaching practice itself. Community-engaged learning should not become symbolic, temporary, or disconnected from community priorities. Educators need to consider how Indigenous knowledge is represented in the classroom, who benefits from the learning experience, and whether relationships continue beyond a single guest lecture, classroom visit, or experiential activity.

Recommendations for Educators

For educators interested in community-guided teaching, the RBR Framework offers several practical starting points. Relationship-building should begin before developing a syllabus, experiential learning activity, guest lecture, or assignment. Meaningful engagement takes time and cannot be rushed to fit semester timelines.

Consultation should continue throughout the process, since community priorities, concerns, and availability may shift. This work also benefits from institutional support, including teaching and learning centres, experiential learning offices, Indigenous initiatives offices, libraries, and administrative partners.

Student preparation is equally important. Before community-engaged learning, students need space to reflect on positionality, colonial histories, respectful engagement, and local protocols. Journaling, discussion, and classroom preparation can help them enter these learning spaces with humility and responsibility.

Finally, instructors need to remain responsive. Community-guided teaching cannot always follow a rigid syllabus or predetermined plan. Elder availability, evolving relationships, and community priorities are central to ethical teaching practice.

Conclusion

Integrating Indigenous perspectives into higher education teaching is not simply a matter of adding content to a syllabus. It requires attention to relationships, responsibilities, community priorities, and guidance. The RBR Framework encourages educators to slow down, listen carefully, and build community-engaged teaching through reciprocity and sustained collaboration. By prioritizing relationships over course design, classroom implementation, and institutional timelines, educators can move beyond symbolic inclusion toward more meaningful teaching and learning.

Acknowledgment: We thank the Curve Lake First Nation community and the Curve Lake First Nation Chief and Council for their support of this work, and in particular Elder Dorothy Taylor and Elder Phyllis Williams, who are the Community Leads for the broader Curve Lake language and cultural documentation and revitalization work.

Carol Ducharme is a Saulteaux community member of Keeseekoose First Nation. She has an interdisciplinary background in Dental Hygiene, Adult Education, Indigenous Education, Indigenous pedagogies, and curriculum integration. Her work is grounded in relational values, lived experience, and the Indigenous perspectives and teachings received through relationships with Elders, Knowledge Keepers, communities, and learners. Her experience spans across post-secondary education, Indigenous community engagement, faculty development, and project management. She currently works in the Indigenous Initiatives Office at the University of Toronto Scarborough.

She holds a Master of Education (Post-Secondary Studies), a Bachelor of Education (Aboriginal Adult Education), and a Diploma in Dental Hygiene, along with additional training in health, mental health, and trauma-informed approaches. In her university-facing work, she supports faculty in integrating Indigenous perspectives, knowledge, and pedagogies into curriculum, teaching practice, and student learning experiences.

Sharing knowledge and responsibilities is a central motivator in her work. She supports learning spaces where Indigenous knowledge is approached with humility, accountability, respect, and reciprocity. In a previous role as Assistant Director of Indigenous Initiatives at the University of Toronto, she supported reconciliation-focused initiatives, Indigenous programming, and a community language revitalization project with Curve Lake First Nation.

Dr. Safieh Moghaddam (PhD, University of Toronto) is an Associate Professor (Teaching Stream) of Linguistics in the Department of Language Studies at the University of Toronto Scarborough (UTSC). Her research concentrates on sociolinguistics (the interaction of language, culture, gender, and race/ethnicity), linguistic typology and universals (the documentation of minority and endangered languages, as well as the syntax and morphology of endangered and less-studied languages). In the classroom, she focuses on active and cooperative learning and on course design for hybrid (dual delivery) and fully online formats. She has developed and redesigned undergraduate courses at all levels, aligning assessments with clear learning outcomes and creating learner-centered syllabi and activities. Her teaching approach emphasizes consistent, actionable feedback and strong student-instructor relationships to foster engagement, equity, and student success.
