I was that student.

I was an adult learner balancing a full-time job, raising children, managing bills, and pursuing a doctoral degree during a global pandemic. Within one year, I lost both of my grandparents. Life was happening in real time—grief, uncertainty, and emotional exhaustion—while the expectation remained unchanged: show up, perform, submit.

But I did not have anything left to give.

In many of my classes, I felt invisible—just a name on a roster, another assignment in the gradebook. Eventually, I had to step away from my program, not because I lacked motivation, but because I lacked capacity.

When I returned, one professor changed everything.

She cared—genuinely.

She reached out. She was patient. She created space for me to be human while still holding me accountable. That experience reshaped how I view teaching. I decided in that moment: I would become the kind of educator I needed when I was struggling.

Now, as an instructor, I see clearly—students are not lazy. They are navigating lives we do not always see.

What Trauma Looks Like in the Online Classroom

Trauma does not always present itself in obvious ways. In higher education—particularly in online learning environments—it often shows up as behavior.

Students:

Apologize excessively for circumstances beyond their control

Disappear instead of communicating

Shut down after missing deadlines or falling short of expectations

Avoid engagement due to fear of judgment or failure

These behaviors are frequently misinterpreted as a lack of effort or disinterest. In reality, they often reflect overwhelm, fear, or survival responses.

As illustrated in the poem “’Cause I Ain’t Got a Pencil” by Joshua T. Dickerson (1991), what appears as unpreparedness is often the result of unseen hardship. Students arrive in our classrooms carrying experiences that shape their ability to participate, perform, and persist.

If we only respond to the behavior, we miss the story behind it.

Equity Is Not the Same as Equality

One of the most common misunderstandings in education is the belief that fairness means treating all students the same.

Equality gives every student the same resources.

Equity recognizes that students are not starting from the same place—and provides what each student needs to succeed.

When we insist on identical expectations without considering individual circumstances, we risk reinforcing inequities rather than addressing them. Trauma-informed teaching is not about lowering standards; it is about removing unnecessary barriers so that students can meet them.

What We Get Wrong as Educators

Too often, higher education equates rigidity with rigor.

We:

Enforce inflexible policies without context

Interpret missed work as laziness

Expect students to “figure it out” independently

Lose sight of our purpose as educators

Over time, the structure of academia can cause us to forget why we began teaching in the first place. Trauma-informed teaching is not an additional responsibility—it is a return to that purpose.

What Trauma-Informed Teaching Looks Like in Practice

Trauma-informed teaching is not theoretical. It is practical, intentional, and immediately applicable.

Here are strategies that consistently work in my classroom:

1. Open, Consistent Communication

From the first day, I tell my students: life happens. Communication matters. Students do not need to overshare, but they do need to keep me informed. When communication is established, support becomes possible.

2. Flexible, Structured Policies

I maintain expectations while allowing flexibility when students communicate. Late work is accepted with accountability. The goal is not perfection—it is persistence.

3. Proactive Outreach

When students disengage or miss assignments, I reach out first. This simple act often re-engages students who might otherwise withdraw completely.

4. Strength-Based Feedback

I use a “sandwich” approach—affirmation, guidance, encouragement. Rather than focusing on what students did wrong, I emphasize how they can improve moving forward. Tone matters. Feedback should build, not break students.

5. Purpose-Driven Motivation

I remind students to remember their “why.” When coursework becomes overwhelming, reconnecting to purpose can sustain effort and resilience.

Why This Matters More in Online Learning

Online learning environments amplify disconnection.

Students:

Lack face-to-face interaction

Are more likely to feel invisible

Can easily misinterpret tone in written communication

Experience increased isolation

In these environments, communication becomes the primary tool for connection. When instructors lead with clarity, empathy, and intentionality, students are more likely to engage and persist.

Tone becomes pedagogy.

What Happens When We Get It Right

When trauma-informed teaching is implemented effectively, the impact is measurable.

Students:

Stay enrolled

Improve academic performance

Communicate more openly

Rebuild confidence

I have had students who failed multiple courses complete mine—not because the content was easier, but because the environment was more accessible.

Research supports this approach. Trauma-informed educational practices have been shown to improve student engagement, retention, and academic outcomes (Carello and Butler 2015; Imad 2021). Additionally, research shows that trauma and stress can significantly impact memory, attention, and overall cognitive functioning, directly affecting a student’s ability to learn (NICABM 2018).

Sometimes, the difference is not the curriculum—it is the connection.

A Question for Educators

For those who believe this approach is not their responsibility, I ask:

What do you want to be remembered for?

Most educators did not enter this profession to enforce policies. They entered it to make an impact. Trauma-informed teaching allows us to reconnect with that purpose.

Conclusion

Students are not showing up empty—they are showing up carrying everything.

When we recognize that—and respond with intention, flexibility, and care—we create learning environments where students can not only succeed academically but continue moving forward in their lives.

They’re not lazy.

They’re navigating life.

And sometimes, what they need most is a professor who sees them.

Dr. Ariel R. Vaughan, PhD, QMHP, is a psychology instructor, published researcher, and trauma-informed educator with a background in counseling and higher education. Drawing from both lived experience and professional practice, she focuses on creating supportive, student-centered learning environments in online and higher-education settings. Her work bridges research and practice by offering practical strategies that improve student engagement, retention, and academic success while recognizing the real-life challenges students navigate.

References

Carello, Janice, and Lisa D. Butler. 2015. “Practicing What We Teach: Trauma-Informed Educational Practice.” Journal of Teaching in Social Work 35 (3): 262–278.

Dickerson, Joshua T. 1991. “’Cause I Ain’t Got a Pencil.”

Imad, Mays. 2021. “A Trauma-Informed Approach to Teaching.” The Chronicle of Higher Education.

National Institute for the Clinical Application of Behavioral Medicine (NICABM). 2018. How Trauma Affects Learning and Behavior.

Community College Loaner Program Leads to Measurable Results

Brightpoint Community College piloted its loaner program back in 2018, lending out Chromebooks. “When the pandemic hit, students were coming to our accommodations office or the dean of students’ office saying, ‘I don’t have a computer. I’m going to fail all my classes,’” Sherry says.

The school had about 60 or 70 devices circulating then, “but the demand was much bigger” and the school ramped up, she says. “Now, we have about 700 in circulation, and last academic year, we loaned devices 1,680 times.”

It made sense for the library to lead the scaling effort. “We know how to do processes and we know how to communicate,” she says. “And we have our integrated library systems, these huge databases where we can check things out to students and we can record where things are.”

READ MORE: Device programs pave the way to digital equity.

As the program grew, the library adjusted staffing. “Now, one of our six full-time positions manages this program. And we have a part-time person who works on this program,” she says.

Others in the school also play a role. “We had to have the lawyers look over our form, because students do lose things, and we wanted to make sure that we could try to get things back,” she says. But they’ll forgive a lost laptop, for example, if there’s a police report or insurance claim showing it was lost in an apartment fire. “We are here for the students to graduate. We want them to do this.”

The loaners are, in part, old faculty and staff devices, classroom laptops that have been repurposed. The effort has had a measurable impact: Year-to-year retention increased more than 7% in students who borrowed library laptops, and credential attainment increased 11%.

“Folks were more concerned about the devices going missing. From a library point of view, devices will go missing. But this is how our students will be successful,” Sherry says. “You can’t let that stop you.”

Lone Star College Program Serves All Students

With more than 20 locations, Lone Star College System made a big pivot during the pandemic. It was a “massive shift” to get all coursework online in a month, says Quentin Wright, president of Lone Star College-Houston North.

But there was an unexpected benefit: Money from the CARES Act helped fund the launch of a device loaner program. Since then, that effort has become institutionalized, serving 31,000 students to date, Wright says.

Having HP and Apple iPad devices available for students to borrow is an essential equity play. “One third of our students are on Pell Grants. We have a significant number of students who are on financial aid. Many of our students work, so finances are an issue,” he says. That’s especially true for first-year students. “We have fairly low tuition, but the books and the supplies can be a shock to students.”

READ MORE: Modern device refresh strategies keep organizations safe.

To pay for the loaner effort beyond the initial CARES Act funding, the school tapped its “special initiatives” budget line. Wright also looked for ways to streamline. To that end, the school launched Community Assistance and Resources for Everyone, or CARE.

“It’s a one-stop shop for students that need help with basic needs,” including access to technology, he says. They can request a loaner device there and also get financial help to buy their own device. “It made it easier for the students, and helped us to institutionalize the program.”

The impact has been clear. From August 2021 through 2025, the cumulative persistence rate for students who participated in the loaner program was 5% higher for students who received devices, according to Wright.

“That’s the whole idea of equity: Meet students where they are and get them to an even playing field,” Wright says. “The fact that these students are performing slightly better, that is a win.”

Device Loaner Program Improves Student Success

Through a partnership between Campus IT and the University Library, California State University, Northridge (CUSN) provides semester-long loans of laptops, tablets and mobile hotspots at no cost to currently enrolled students.

“The device loaner program promotes equity by removing technology access barriers for students who do not own or cannot afford the devices needed for coursework,” says Ryan Conlogue, associate IT vice president.

The University Library had a loaner program before the pandemic, but it expanded significantly during that period. Since then, the program has matured into a permanent, fully operational campus service. It has evolved from a small inventory of short-term loaner devices to “a sustainable, semester-long lending program with dedicated library operations, IT support and ongoing investment,” Conlogue says.

Data helped support the expansion. “Institutional research showing positive impacts on student success has helped demonstrate the program’s value,” he says. That helped to position loaners as “a core component of CSUN’s digital equity and student success strategy.”

DISCOVER: Learn how to manage devices throughout the entire lifecycle.

That research showed that students who borrowed devices earned significantly higher GPAs than nonparticipants, with particularly positive outcomes for Pell-eligible, first-generation, Latino, African American and female students. “Because these groups have historically experienced equity gaps, the program is helping improve the academic conditions that support long-term retention and graduation,” Conlogue says.

Maintaining the program at scale requires a combination of operational processes, technical management and sustainable funding.

“Today, much of the day-to-day logistics are supported by our student assistants, who play a critical role in inventory management, device check-in and check-out, cleaning, testing, and preparing devices for redeployment each semester,” he says. “That work represents a significant operational commitment, particularly during peak periods at the beginning and end of each term.”

From a security and lifecycle perspective, devices is assigned to individual students and are centrally managed, ensuring software, security and institutional configurations stay current, he says.

The biggest outcome: Better equity. “The program helps reduce disparities in educational access that stem from socioeconomic differences,” Conlogue says.

The IT Factor

The university IT team can play a key role in driving the success of a device loaner program. Teams can:

Manage the inventory. “Lone Star College is a very big system. We have over 20 locations, and they work out the logistics of how many devices to keep at a particular site. If we’re oversupplied on one campus, they will move them to another campus,” says Wright.

Provision and maintain devices. At Brightpoint Community College, IT buys and images the Dell devices, “so we’ve got the right software at the right time,” says Sherry.

Drive efficiency. California State University, Northridge is looking streamline its loaner program with automation and improved asset management workflows. “As our tools and processes mature, we’re working to reduce manual effort while maintaining a positive experience for students,” says Conlogue.

title: The future is here: the Ethical and Sustainable Employability Toolkit

Stuart Norton, Advance HE’s Head of Educational Excellence, introduces the new Ethical and Sustainable Employability Toolkit, a Wales-wide initiative funded by Medr and supported by Advance HE.

I’ve been looking forward to sharing this for some time. The Ethical and Sustainable Employability (ESE) Toolkit has now been published, and it represents something genuinely significant for higher education in Wales, and potentially well beyond.

At a time when the nature of work is changing rapidly, employability conversations are also shifting. Graduates are increasingly looking not only for good careers, but for work that aligns with their values and contributes to a fairer, more sustainable world. The ESE Toolkit responds directly to this shift, offering practical ways for institutions to embed ethical and sustainable thinking within employability practice.

A whole-nation collaboration

One of the most encouraging aspects of this project is the way it has been developed: collaboratively, across Wales. Rather than a single institutional initiative, this has been a pan-Wales effort involving higher education providers across the country, supported through funding from Medr (the Commission for Tertiary Education and Research) and with secretariat support from Advance HE.

There is something powerful about seeing institutions work collectively in this way. When the sector shares expertise and learning, the impact is far greater than anything achieved in isolation. It has been a privilege to work alongside colleagues across Wales who have contributed their expertise, ideas and examples of practice.

A practical toolkit

What stands out immediately is that this is not a conceptual report destined for a shelf. It is a genuinely practical resource. The toolkit offers a clear five-stage pathway for institutions seeking to develop ethical and sustainable employability:

Audit

Identify and Establish

Scale

Implement and Evaluate

Contribute

It is grounded in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and importantly in the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, a globally distinctive piece of legislation that asks public bodies in Wales to think about the long-term consequences of decisions for people, communities and the planet. Embedding this perspective within employability helps frame careers not simply as individual success stories, but as contributions to wider social and environmental futures.

Learning from practice

One of the strongest aspects of the toolkit is the collection of case studies from across Welsh higher education. These move beyond theory and show how ethical and sustainable employability can be realised in practice. Examples include:

Marketing for Good (Swansea University) – where students work on live briefs for organisations such as Wales Air Ambulance and the Wildlife Trust, applying digital marketing skills to social impact.

The Sustainathon (Open University) – a week-long challenge where students tackle real sustainability issues while building confidence, curiosity and collaborative skills.

Places of Climate Change (Bangor University) – an interdisciplinary initiative combining seminars, workshops and internships focused on climate action.

Interdisciplinary Hackathons – where students use the Well-being of Future Generations Act as a catalyst for developing innovative responses to policy and sustainability challenges.

Across teaching, careers services and institutional leadership, the toolkit provides a range of ideas that can be adapted to different contexts, from carbon literacy initiatives to ethical careers policies that help students navigate values-based career choices.

Why this matters

For anyone thinking seriously about the future of employability in higher education, this toolkit is well worth exploring. It offers a thoughtful and practical framework for aligning graduate outcomes with wider societal priorities. For me personally, it has also been a pleasure to see this work develop over the past 18 months, emerging from the Wales Employability Community of Practice and building on earlier work in this space.

If you are interested in ethical and sustainable employability, I would encourage you to take a look and share it with colleagues. The team at Swansea University is also keen to gather further examples of practice, so there is an opportunity for this to continue growing as institutions contribute their own work.

by Yaz Iyabo Osho

Academic professional development (APD) has a central role in supporting teaching and learning in higher education. Through development programmes, workshops, resources, professional networks, and opportunities to share practice, colleagues are supported in developing their knowledge, expertise, and ideas.

I have long been interested in another aspect of academic professional development: what it can help us understand about educational practice, student experience, and the particularities of higher education institutions. When universities encounter challenges relating to inclusion, belonging, student engagement, or educational outcomes, how do we determine what kind of development or support is needed? What critically informs those decisions? Whose knowledge and experiences are considered? And what can we learn from what happens afterwards?

These questions underpin an approach I am developing as ‘Research-Informed Academic Professional Development’ (Research-Informed APD). My interest is in how academic professional development can contribute not only to supporting practice, but also to generating and connecting knowledge that informs educational decision-making and institutional learning.

The foundations of my thinking

Although I am now giving this approach a name, its foundations have developed over several years of my research and professional practice. Earlier in my career, working in widening-participation higher education contexts, I became increasingly interested in how students’ experiences could inform our understanding of engagement, progression and success. In my earlier writing on widening participation and enterprise education (Osho, nd), I argued for greater attention to institutional practices and approaches to teaching and learning, rather than focusing on perceived deficiencies among students.

This thinking continued through collaborative research exploring the experiences behind ethnic minority students’ attainment (Seuwou et al, 2023), alongside my own work on racialised awarding gaps and inclusive curriculum practices. Several of my studies were subsequently referenced in the University of Westminster’s Access and Participation Plan (2025–2029), contributing to the institutional evidence base for understanding educational inequalities and informing approaches to curriculum development and inclusion. Later in my career, my responsibilities as an EDI Lead brought together research, colleague development, inclusive and anti-racist pedagogy, curriculum enhancement, and evaluation.

More recently, moving into an institution-wide academic professional development role allowed me to consider these questions across different disciplines, professional roles and institutional contexts at scale. It also made me think more about how knowledge can be generated through educational practice. Looking across my work, I can see a consistent interest in understanding educational questions before deciding how best to respond. Research-Informed APD is the name I am now giving to an approach that has developed through this research and practice over several years.

Building on established scholarship

The idea that academic professional development should extend beyond individual activities is not new. I am interested in what academic professional development can help institutions understand about their educational practices, beyond the programmes, resources and support it provides.

Research-Informed APD is the name I am giving to an approach that has emerged through my research, professional practice and reflections on the purposes of academic professional development. This requires us to look beyond responding to immediate educational challenges and consider what we might learn through the process.

Her research interests include inclusive and anti-racist pedagogy, academic professional development, CPD governance, belonging, and the experiences of Black students and academics in higher education. title: 5 Impulse zur KI-Transformation von der Learning AID
summary:
In der Praxis ist KI an vielen Hochschulen längst angekommen – die institutionelle Einbettung hält damit nicht immer Schritt. Anja Westermann und Jens Tobor nehmen einen gemeinsam mit Malte Miram gestalteten Workshop auf der Learning AID zum Ausgangspunkt und formulieren fünf Impulse für institutionelle Handlungsfähigkeit.

The post 5 Impulse zur KI-Transformation von der Learning AID appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Beim Thema KI geht es an Hochschulen längst nicht mehr nur um das Starten neuer Pilotprojekte, Lehrformate, KI-Tools und Unterstützungsangebote. Die Aufgabe, die immer stärker in den Vordergrund rückt, lautet, aus den verteilten Initiativen und Impulsen ein gemeinsames Verständnis und eine kohärente strategische Handlungsfähigkeit zu entwickeln. Denn KI wirkt tief in akademische wie organisatorische Abläufe hinein und erfordert eine gezielte Steuerung, damit zentrale Prinzipien wie wissenschaftliche Integrität und institutionelles Selbstverständnis gewahrt bleiben.

Genau diese Dynamik spiegelte sich auch am 01. September wider, als die Community rund um Lernen, Lehren und Technologie auf der Learning AID zusammenkam. Für uns ist die Konferenz jedes Jahr ein wunderbarer Seismograph der sozio-technischen Transformation der Hochschulbildung.

Gemeinsam durften wir vor Ort unseren Workshop „KI-Transformation gestalten: Strategien, Praxis und Governance teilen und gemeinsam weiterdenken“ moderieren. In vier Themengruppen und einem lebendigen Plenum haben die 36 Teilnehmenden geteilt, wo Hochschulen aktuell stehen, wo es hakt und welche Lösungen sich bewähren. Der Workshop knüpfte nahtlos an die Atmosphäre der Learning AID an: Den Teilnehmenden merkten wir die Bereitschaft an, voneinander zu lernen und über Fach- und Institutionsgrenzen hinweg zu kooperieren.

Um diese vielfältigen Eindrücke weiterzutragen, führen wir die Kernbotschaften aus unserem Workshop und der Tagung hier im Blog zusammen.

Als Ausgangspunkt für die Arbeitsphase gaben wir den Teilnehmenden Einblicke in aktuelle Beobachtungen des Hochschulforums Digitalisierung. Sie basieren auf Erkenntnissen aus den Peer-to-Peer-Strategieberatungen, dem KI-Lab und Publikationen wie dem Blickpunkt „Leitlinien-Check 2026“ oder dem Arbeitspapier „KI als Managementaufgabe der Hochschule“. Dabei zeigt sich, dass die anfänglich oft ablehnende und abwehrende Haltung an den Hochschulen einer Phase der konstruktiven Auseinandersetzung gewichen ist. An vielen Hochschulen existieren bereits Leitlinien, vielerorts werden Tool-Lizenzen erprobt sowie institutionelle KI-Zugänge bereitgestellt und Pilotprojekte gestartet.

Doch die eigentliche Arbeit beginnt erst jetzt: Nach der ersten Phase des Erprobens gilt es nun, die Folgen für die gesamte Institution zu reflektieren und organisatorisch aufzugreifen. Wie lassen sich Selbstverständnis und Werte der Hochschulbildung in einer Zeit bewahren und weiterentwickeln, in der KI-Systeme genau diese Fundamente herausfordern? Um diese Frage greifbar zu machen, haben wir sie über vier Spannungsfelder konkretisiert:

Viele KI-Aktivitäten beginnen als Pilot, Drittmittelprojekt oder Initiative einzelner Engagierter. Für Erforschung, Erkundung und Innovation einer dynamischen Technologie mag das sinnvoll sein. Problematisch wird es dort, wo aus einer vorläufigen Lösung unbemerkt eine projektförmige Dauerlösung wird: Ein Tool wird genutzt, eine Beratung nachgefragt oder ein Service erwartet, ohne dass Personal, Finanzierung und Zuständigkeit für den dauerhaften Betrieb geklärt sind. Wird dieser Bogen überspannt, kann es sein, dass potenziell gute Lösungen ganz verschwinden. Ein Anlass, die Lage eingesetzter KI‑Technologien an der Hochschule überhaupt erst einmal zu sondieren, kann die laut AI‑Act formulierte Anforderung sein, KI-Inventare aufzustellen und zu pflegen.

KI als Daueraufgabe ernst zu nehmen bedeutet auch, zu entscheiden, welche Angebote inzwischen in den Regelbetrieb gehören, weil sie von Hochschulangehörigen erwartet werden, und welche Leistungen darüber hinaus strategisch sinnvoll sind und gegebenenfalls zur Profilbildung beitragen. Um einen Regelbetrieb zu gewährleisten, sind etwa verlässliche KI-Zugänge, Qualifizierung, Beratung, technische Betreuung oder Verfahren zur Bewertung neuer Anwendungen sinnvoll.

Einige dieser Funktionen müssen dabei nicht zwingend allein hochschulintern organisiert werden – darauf kommen wir im fünften Impuls zurück. Kurzum: Neben den weiterhin wichtigen Experimentierräumen brauchen Hochschulen ebenso Mechanismen, mit denen aus bewährten Experimenten belastbare Strukturen entstehen. Die Herausforderung besteht damit in einer doppelten Bewegung, die Bewährtes verstetigen kann, ohne die Fähigkeit zum pragmatischen Erproben und schnellen Handeln zu verlieren.

Genau diese Beweglichkeit können pragmatische Quick-Wins schaffen. Gerade weil die KI-Transformation einen langen Atem braucht, sind überschaubare, schnell wirksame Verbesserungen wichtig: ein vereinfachter Verwaltungsprozess, eine gut funktionierende Prompt-Sammlung, ein erprobtes Schulungsformat oder eine lokale Lösung, die sich ohne großen Aufwand übertragen lässt. Solche Quick-Wins schaffen konkreten Nutzen, machen Fortschritt sichtbar und können Akzeptanz für größere strukturelle Veränderungen stärken.

Sie sind damit mehr als Motivationshilfen: Unter Unsicherheit ermöglichen sie es, ins Handeln zu kommen, Erfahrungen zu sammeln und daraus die nächsten Schritte abzuleiten. Nicht jeder erfolgreiche Versuch muss dabei unmittelbar skaliert werden. Entscheidend ist, aus ihm zu lernen. Damit aus diesen Erfahrungen wiederum mehr wird als eine Ansammlung lokaler Einzelaktivitäten, müssen sie innerhalb der Hochschule sichtbar werden und bestenfalls so aufbereitet werden, dass erkennbar wird, unter welchen Bedingungen etwas funktioniert hat und was sich daraus für weitere Entscheidungen ableiten lässt.

Wer ist eigentlich zuständig, wenn didaktische, technische, rechtliche und strategische Fragen gleichzeitig berührt werden? Die Workshopdiskussionen zeigten, dass das Problem häufig weniger das vollständige Fehlen von Strukturen ist als unklare Verantwortungsübergänge, stockende Informationsflüsse und fehlende Verbindungen zwischen dezentralem Erfahrungswissen und zentralen Entscheidungen. Hochschulen sind keine fein verzahnten Maschinen, sondern eher ein Geflecht relativ eigenständiger Bereiche. Die entscheidende Governancefrage lautet daher, wie tragfähige Brücken zwischen diesen Bereichen geschaffen werden können.

Die Aufgabe besteht darin, solche Verbindungen gezielt herzustellen und zu stärken, ohne dabei die Frage nach Zuständigkeiten und Entscheidungsrechten allein auf ein Kommunikationsproblem zu verkürzen. Denn hochschulweite AI-Readiness entsteht nicht allein durch technische Ausstattung oder Einzelkompetenzen, sondern auch dadurch, dass Herausforderungen, Lösungsansätze und Lernerfahrungen zwischen Bereichen zirkulieren und in Entscheidungen einfließen können.

Neue organisationale Einheiten wie AI Offices können dabei als Koordinations- und Übersetzungsknoten dienen: Sie bündeln verteilte Expertise, machen Bedarfe und Entwicklungen sichtbar und bereiten sie so auf, dass sie organisationsweite Entscheidungen unterstützt. Gleichzeitig dürfen sie nicht zu Orten werden, an die Verantwortungsübernahme und Expertise exklusiv ausgelagert werden.

Die Existenz eines solchen Office entlastet die Leitungsebene beispielsweise nicht davon, eigene KI-Kompetenzen zu entwickeln, wie Workshopteilnehmende herausstellten: Wer über KI-bezogene Fragen im Kontext der Hochschulentwicklung entscheiden soll, muss die Konsequenzen dieser Entscheidungen zumindest hinreichend einschätzen können. Mit funktionierenden Informationswegen ist allerdings noch nicht geklärt, wessen Perspektiven über diese Wege überhaupt in Entscheidungen Eingang finden sollten.

Studierende gehören bei der KI-Transformation nicht nur deshalb an den Tisch, weil Beteiligung grundsätzlich wünschenswert ist. Sie verfügen über Erfahrungswissen, das für gute Entscheidungen unverzichtbar ist: Wie wird KI im Studienalltag tatsächlich eingesetzt? Wo entstehen Unsicherheiten? Welche Regeln werden verstanden, welche umgangen? Wo entstehen neue Unterschiede beim Zugang oder in der Nutzung? Ein offener Umgang mit diesen Fragen setzt tatsächliches Erkenntnisinteresse und eine nachvollziehbare Rückkopplung in Entscheidungen voraus und funktioniert nur, wenn eine faktisch breite KI-Nutzung (vgl. Horstmann et al. 2026) enttabuisiert diskutiert werden kann.

Das Gleiche gilt für Lehrende, Supporteinrichtungen, Verwaltung und andere Akteursgruppen. Wer strategische Leitlinien, Curricula oder Prüfungsregelungen entwickelt, braucht Zugang zu diesem verteilten Erfahrungswissen. Partizipation ist deshalb nicht bloß Legitimation, sondern auch eine Voraussetzung organisationaler Beobachtungs- und Entscheidungsfähigkeit.

Gleichzeitig genügt es nicht, immer dieselben engagierten Vertreter:innen einzubeziehen. Gerade bei Studierenden muss gefragt werden, wie die Vielfalt unterschiedlicher Lebensrealitäten, Studienbedingungen und KI-Nutzungsweisen überhaupt sichtbar werden kann. Damit verschiebt sich die Frage von „Wer darf mitreden?“ zu: Welche Perspektiven fehlen uns bislang – und wie können wir sie einbeziehen, um fundiert darüber zu entscheiden, welche Rolle KI an der Hochschule spielen soll?

Dieses Prinzip verteilten Erfahrungswissens endet allerdings nicht an den Grenzen der eigenen Hochschule. Gerade bei Infrastruktur, Spezialexpertise und Support stellt sich auch hochschulübergreifend die Frage, was gemeinsam besser geleistet werden kann.

Kaum eine Hochschule wird die für KI nötige Infrastruktur, Expertise und Unterstützungslandschaft allein aufbauen und aktuell halten können. Hochschulverbünde und überregionale Kooperationen können deshalb helfen, Ressourcen zu bündeln, technische Lösungen gemeinsam zu betreiben und spezialisierte Expertise verfügbar zu machen.

Kooperation bedeutet jedoch nicht, Verantwortung auszulagern oder sich allein auf die KI-Expertise starker Verbundpartner:innen zu verlassen. Stattdessen müssen alle Kooperationspartner:innen institutionell selbst entscheiden können, welche Lösungen zu den eigenen Zielen, Fachkulturen und Anforderungen an Daten und Prozesse passen.

Dafür müssen sie nicht jede Spezialexpertise selbst vorhalten, aber über genügend eigene Urteilskraft verfügen, um Anforderungen zu formulieren, Optionen zu bewerten und über Einsatz oder Nicht-Einsatz informiert entscheiden zu können. Kooperation erweitert somit Handlungsspielräume, darf aber gerade die institutionelle Handlungsfähigkeit kleinerer Partner:innen nicht schwächen. Umgekehrt stärkt deren eigene Urteils- und Integrationsfähigkeit nämlich auch die Kooperation selbst.

Die Learning AID hat einmal mehr gezeigt: Die Hochschul-Community wartet nicht ab, sondern gestaltet längst pragmatisch, kritisch und lösungsorientiert. Zwischen strategischer Ausrichtung, technischer Infrastruktur und didaktischer Praxis gibt es dabei keine einfachen Abkürzungen. Was es stattdessen braucht, ist Mut zum Ausprobieren, transparente Kommunikation auf Augenhöhe und vor allem den festen Willen, diesen Weg nicht allein zu gehen.

Die KI-Transformation ist ein Marathon, kein Sprint. Doch sie wird spürbar leichter, wenn wir Erfahrungen, Erfolge und auch das Scheitern kontinuierlich miteinander teilen. Hochschulen, die jetzt auf Kooperation setzen, verbindliche Verantwortlichkeiten etablieren und Studierende als aktive Mitgestalter:innen begreifen, legen ein belastbares Fundament für künftige Innovationswellen.

Für uns als HFD-Team war die Konferenz eine wunderbare Bestätigung dafür, mit wie viel Energie und Offenheit dieser Diskurs geführt wird. Wir freuen uns darauf, diesen Weg gemeinsam mit der Community weiterzugehen!

title: Por la defensa de la educación, la soberanía y la democracia
summary:
Quinta Marcha Universitaria en Argentina

La entrada Por la defensa de la educación, la soberanía y la democracia se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
El jueves 15 de octubre, la Argentina vuelve a movilizarse en defensa de la universidad pública. La Quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria reúne a estudiantes, docentes, trabajadoras y trabajadores no docentes, autoridades universitarias y organizaciones sociales y sindicales en una jornada que trasciende los reclamos específicos del sistema educativo y expresa una preocupación compartida por el presente y el futuro del país.

Bajo la consigna “Por la defensa de la educación, la soberanía y la democracia”,esta movilización es la continuación de un conflicto que se ha intensificado debido a la falta de aplicación de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario sancionada por el Congreso a fines de 2025 y que el gobierno libertariano de Javier Milei se niega a aplicar.

La movilización, de la que participan distintos integrantes de la Red CLACSO, reclama el cumplimiento efectivo de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, la recomposición de los salarios docentes y no docentes, la actualización de las becas estudiantiles y los recursos necesarios para garantizar el funcionamiento de las universidades nacionales y la continuidad del sistema científico.

La convocatoria se produce, además, en el contexto del debate sobre el Presupuesto 2027 con más recortes a las partidas destinadas a educación y de las demandas por el cumplimiento de las decisiones judiciales vinculadas con el financiamiento universitario que el gobierno argentino incumplió en reiteradas oportunidades.

La jornada coincide con otras expresiones de la conflictividad social argentina. A las demandas de la comunidad universitaria se suman las reivindicaciones de distintos sectores del movimiento sindical, las organizaciones sociales y los colectivos que reclaman respuestas frente al endeudamiento de los hogares, la emergencia en discapacidad y el deterioro de las condiciones de vida.

Esta convergencia permite reconocer un punto de encuentro entre reivindicaciones diversas: la defensa de los derechos sociales y de las condiciones materiales que hacen posible una vida digna. El acceso a la educación, la estabilidad laboral, los ingresos, la salud, la inclusión, el respeto a las discapacidades y la producción de conocimiento no son dimensiones aisladas. Forman parte de una trama de derechos interdependientes que inciden directamente en las posibilidades de desarrollo de las personas y de la sociedad en su conjunto.

La universidad pública ocupa un lugar central en esa trama. Es un espacio de formación, investigación, pensamiento crítico y producción de conocimientos; una institución que amplía oportunidades, favorece la movilidad social y contribuye a comprender y transformar la realidad. Su fortalecimiento también resulta decisivo para la capacidad de los países de América Latina y el Caribe de producir conocimientos propios, desarrollar ciencia y tecnología y construir proyectos de futuro con mayor autonomía.

La defensa de la universidad pública remite, por lo tanto, a una discusión más amplia sobre el papel del Estado, las responsabilidades públicas y el lugar de la educación y la ciencia en el desarrollo de nuestras sociedades. Cuando las demandas universitarias convergen con las de otros sectores sociales, se vuelve visible la relación entre el financiamiento de las instituciones públicas, las condiciones de trabajo, la igualdad de oportunidades y la garantía de derechos.

Desde una perspectiva nuestroamericana, estas discusiones también interpelan a la región en su conjunto. Las universidades públicas y los sistemas científicos –atacados y desfinanciados en varios países de la región– constituyen bienes estratégicos para enfrentar las desigualdades, fortalecer las democracias y generar respuestas colectivas a los desafíos sociales, económicos, culturales y ambientales contemporáneos.

La quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria en Argentina vuelve a colocar estas cuestiones en el espacio público. Su significado no se limita a una disputa presupuestaria: expresa la preocupación por las condiciones que permiten sostener una sociedad con derechos, ampliar las oportunidades de las nuevas generaciones y construir un horizonte compartido.

ll caldo record di quest’estate sta facendo crescere la consapevolezza che il verde urbano non è un elemento accessorio e ornamentale ma un’infrastruttura necessaria per rendere vivibili città in cui asfalto, inquinamento, traffico e condizionatori d’aria intensificano i picchi di temperature e le ondate di calore. Gli alberi svolgono una funzione fondamentale nella regolazione delle temperature e nella qualità dell’aria, per non parlare della difesa del suolo. Ma, come per ogni infrastruttura «serve pianificazione, manutenzione e continuità dei finanziamenti», spiega Sandro Scollato, amministratore delegato di AzzeroCO2.

Il Pnrr ha concentrato in pochi anni risorse e capacità progettuali sulla forestazione urbana e periurbana delle 14 Città metropolitane. Ma un albero non produce i suoi effetti subito. Nei primi anni servono irrigazione, cure, controlli e sostituzione delle piante che non attecchiscono. È la fase più delicata, soprattutto con estati come quella appena trascorsa. La misura ne teneva conto: tra i requisiti c’era un piano di coltivazione di 5 anni, con sostituzioni, irrigazione, taglio della flora spontanea e trattamenti necessari all’attecchimento e allo sviluppo. La sfida del post-Pnrr è far rispettare questi obblighi fino alla fine del periodo previsto, evitando che ritardi, problemi nella gestione dei contratti o carenze nei controlli compromettano la sopravvivenza delle nuove piante.

Come si fa a passare a interventi che rendano strutturale l’investimento nel verde pubblico?

Il Pnrr ha dimostrato che la concentrazione di risorse, obiettivi e scadenze può accelerare gli interventi, ma ora quella spinta va portata nella programmazione ordinaria delle città, altrimenti si rischia un effetto “scalino”: una crescita rapida delle piantumazioni, seguita da un calo delle risorse quando aumenta il bisogno di cura e continuità. Il verde urbano va trattato come le altre infrastrutture: tutelato da norme, sostenuto da risorse pluriennali per la manutenzione, gestito da competenze tecniche specifiche e inserito nella pianificazione urbanistica.
